Some Surprisingly Sensible Points About Why Some Xbone 1st Party Games are Coming to PC and Others Aren't

I think you linked to the wrong article because I couldn't find the "surprisingly sensible arguments". Releasing AAA titles exclusively for console X only hampers the industry. Check out TotalBiscuits take on it on his E3 thoughts for some well founded argument against any type of console exclusives.

That wasn't what he said at all. His argument was that adding in another platform part way through a development cycle creates unnecessary complications for the development team. Ergo, they aren't going to put that pressure on anyone for a game already built as a first party exclusive. However, once those games are done, there's a stronger probability of seeing ports to Windows than there was before. Also, that future titles are more likely to see Xbone and PC releases from the get-go. The argument that first party exclusives benefit no-one is patently incorrect. Doing precisely that is, has been and will continue to be the crux of Nintendo's success. First party exclusives drive the sale of hardware. Without them, there's a huge reduction in impetus to purchase one piece of hardware over another

That's exactly the point; that the need to purchase a certain console ought to be reduced. My point was not that they should add them on the fly. My point was, why do you release a AAA title without crosa platform support in the first place? I'm not saying that indie developers should release their stuff for every platform because budget, I am however saying that a game developer like Bungie has no excuse for doing so. I wouldn't really call Nintendo a AAA production for any of their games, it's more a case of a style and smart usage of the system. A game like Wii Sports would not do well on anything without the Wii controllers. Any game for Xbox and PS, would. Having exclusive releases is saying "hey, we made this great game, but it's not for everyone even though it easily could be, we just want to force you to give us more money so you can belong to our back-patting group".

Why do you want the focus to move away from hardware? If that happens, there'll be no impetus to make newer, more powerful tech. And again, I repeatedly stated first party. Games made by a company (ie Microsoft) to be sold on their console. Why is that an issue for you? Sure, it sucks that you have to get more kit to play all the games you want, but they're a business and they want to make money. Them's the breaks

Several reasons: It limits the customers' abilities to enjoy a larger landscape of games. What do you think the movie world would look like if you had 4 different types of movie media and if you don't have your betamax machine for 400$ you can't watch one fourth of the movies that exists? Secondly, it becomes a "I have it, and you don't, nananananaaaaana" à la Cartman. Those who can only afford one gaming machine will never be able to enjoy many of the titles released exclusively. Third, it's come to a point where AAA titles not being released to several consoles is not a question of technological ability, it's about laziness. Finally, it's not making sense to alienate a huge chunk of your gaming audience just because you want to sell a few extra consoles. Granted, they're not selling the consoles for profit but rather so that you will purchase more games from them in the future, however most people who don't own their console will think "oh great, another game not being released for my platform, screw those guys", and not want to deal with that developer again. They are a business, yes, so it should be in their interest to reach a larger audience.

Again, I'm talking specifically about in house, first party games made by the company selling the console in the first place. You seem determined to gloss over that aspect in favour of no exclusivity at all. But you hit the nail on the head. They don't (except Nintendo) sell their consoles for profit. Whilst companies that sell DVD players and the like, they do make a profit on their hardware sales. So there clearly is an imperative to steer people towards their brand over another. Sadly, that's where the movie analogy falls down.

Yes, for third party titles, especially the really big companies, it really is idiotic to limit to one platform. Even, I'd say, in the case of a game like Zombi U, which at last had some logic behind being a third party exclusive. But it keeps coming back to the same thing. The video-game industry is driven by profits. Which console manufacturers make by giving an incentive to purchase their console over a competitor. Just like Nvidia do with PhysX for the PC crowd. So again, specifically, why do you oppose first party exclusivity? What would you levy as an alternative method for Microsoft or Sony to make their money? They have to sell consoles somehow, or they might as well stop making them all together and just go to PC. Which would be great, sure, but won't happen. So, what's your alternative?

I agree that it's their end goal of these companies to make money, and since they are making money selling their exclusive games it would seem to make sense to also force users onto their console. However, if they make money selling games, regardless if it's first or third party titles, they would also make money selling them to a larger audience, not limited to their loss-making console. They can still sell the games at a high markup, only now to the many instead of to the few. If we also agreed on that they're not making money on the console but rather the potential games sales in the future, then these manufacturers would still make profits with open platform games. I'm not opposed to the idea itself, I simply think that it is a backwards practice and I doubt that they would not make profits if the titles were open platform.

In an ideal world, yeah, that would be more profitable. But you hit the nail on the head earlier. A lot of people can't afford more than one platform to game on. Or rather, they think they can't because they blow all their cash on games for that platform, but that's another story. Anyway, they tie themselves into one console, and thus make all of their gaming purchases on said platform. Which means the original seller, though supposedly making a loss on their hardware (I still doubt that, but again, another story) are then making a profit not only on sales of their own games, but via the license fee from the sale of every other game on their console. That's why games on consoles cost more than PC. Approximately 20% of the cost of a new game is going to the console manufacturer.

I want to make very clear, I'm not saying that it's right. The exact opposite in fact. It's an extremely anti-consumer business model. But the cold, hard truth of the matter is that it works, and is inevitably far more profitable for far less effort. Unless you can get yourself to the point of being a massive, industry respected developer like, say, Ubisoft (which Microsoft probably could, but not so much Sony) then the console model is far more lucrative. Especially considering it basically generates money for nothing. Much in the same way that Valve never need to do anything at all, they just rake in cash from everyone else selling stuff on Steam

There was a very interesting documentary on that exact thing on BBC called The Secrets of Superbrands, in three episodes. The first one discussed technology and they brought up the PS3. Sony, Microsoft or Nintendo doesn't release the exact figure for the cost of making these products, but in the show they broke it down into separate hardware pieces and found that even just the hardware pieces by themselves cost more than what they were selling the PS3 for. Granted, in their case, Sony had a piece of the pie in the Blueray/HDDVD fight, so providing a Bluray player into everyone's homes would benefit their overall sales. However, I doubt that the makers are making a lot of profit on the console even nowadays.

It seems that we are agreeing here, only that we're presenting our arguments differently. I'll have to call this the end of the discussion, thank you for providing clear and well-founded arguments. I now better understand the reasons for the first party developers using exclusive titles, even though I don't necessarily agree with the reasons.

I still find that questionable personally. I can't shake the thought they were conflating value and cost. After all, something might be "worth" $200, but people might only be willing to pay $50. But yeah, I agree it sucks, I'm only saying there's a firm, business logic behind the model.
